text: Dental Materials Journal 11 (2): 119-129, 1992 119 The Corrosion Behavior of Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 Magnets Asahi KITSUGI*, Osamu OKUNO**, Tsuyoshi NAKANO***, Hitoshi HAMANAKA*** and Takayuki KURODA* *Second Department of Orthodontics , School of Dentistry, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, 1-5-45, Yushima, Bunkyou-Ku, Tokyo, 113, Japan **Division of Metallurgy , Institute for Medical and Dental Engineering, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, 2-3-10, Kanda-Surugadai, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo, 101, Japan Present Address: Department of Dental Materials Science, Tohoku University School of Dentistry, 4-1, Seiryo-machi, Aoba-Ku, Sendai, 980, Japan *** Division of Metallurgy , Institute for Medical and Dental Engineering, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, 2-3-10, Kandasurugadai, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo, 101, Japan Received on July 15, 1992 Accepted on October 29, 1992 Rare earth magnets have corrosive problems associated with their use in prostheses in various fields including orthodontics. The purpose of this study is to investigate the corrosion behavior of an Nd2Fe14B magnet and a SmCo5 magnet in an oral environment. The relations among the attractive force changes, the released elements, the weight changes and the anodic polarization measurements of the magnets were examined under immersions in 1% NaCl, 1% lactic acid, 0.05% HCl, 0.1% Na2S and Greenwood's artificial saliva at 37•Ž for forty-two days. The results showed that the rare earth magnets underwent high corrosive assaults and large attractive force reductions by the immersions in 1% lactic acid and 0.05% HCl. The problem of corrosion of the magnets could be overcome by sealing them within laser-welded stainless steel capsules. Key words: Corrosion, Nd2Fe14B magnet, SmCo5 magnet INTRODUCTION Rare earth magnets, which possess the most superior magnetic properties, have been applied to various dental prostheses1-6). In the field of orthodontics, there have been attempts to use them as effective appliances as well7-15). However, it was reported that the oral cavity was such a corrosive environment that rare earth magnets might corrode easily16-18). Tsutsui et al.16) described that the weight loss of Sm-Co magnets was relatively large in 1% lactic acid and 0.05% HCl. Vardimon et al.17) demonstrated from their electrochemical experiments that rare earth magnets were easy to oxidize. Nakano et al.18) observed that Sm-Co magnets released many Co and Sm ions in 1% lactic acid and 0.05% HCl. These phenomena were investigated independently by the different types of Sm-Co magnets. There is no information concerning the relation between the corrosion behavior and the attractive force of a SmCo5 magnet. There has also been no previous report of the corrosion tendencies of Nd2Fe14B magnets which are superior to SmCo5 magnets in terms of magnetic properties. The purpose of this investigation was to comprehensively characterize the corrosion behavior of both the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets in an oral environment. The corrosion resistances of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets were examined by the attractive force changes, the released elements, the weight changes and the anodic polarization measurements under 120 A. KITSUGI, O. OKUNO, T. NAKANO, H. HAMANAKA and T. KURODA immersions in dental corrosive solutions at 37•Ž. The effect of sealing with laser-welded stainless steel on SmCo5 magnet corrosion was also investigated. Corrosive solutions The corrosive solutions used were 1% NaCl, 1% lactic acid, 0.05% HCl, 0.1% Na2S and Greenwood's artificial saliva, which are often used for the corrosion test of the usual dental alloys20). They were washed in acetone by ultrasonic cleaning equipment. One test piece was put into each vial filled with 20ml of either 1% lactic acid or the artificial saliva. They were kept at 37•}0.5 •Ž for forty-two days. The temperature of the solution was kept constant in a water bath. The attractive force between the magnets was measured by a micro tensile testing device21) at one, three, five, seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight, thirty-five and forty-two days. Before being measured, the specimens were rinsed in pure water and completely dried. 2) Element release test and weight change test The dimensions of the specimens were cylinders of 10.0mm in diameter and 4.0mm in thickness. They were cleaned in acetone by ultrasonic cleaning equipment. Each specimen was immersed in one of the five kinds of corrosive solutions of 20ml filling the vials. No corrosive solutions were exchanged, and all were kept at 37•}0.5•Ž in the water bath. The released elements were measured by inductively coupled plasma emission spectrometry (ICP) at one, three, seven and twenty-eight days. The specimens were weighed at the same time of their immersions. Before weighing, the specimens were rinsed in pure water and dried in a desiccator until the weight reached a constant value. In both of the tests, the final values were the average of five tests. 3) Anodic polarization measurement The specimens were cylinders of 4.0mm in diameter and 1.5mm in thickness. They were burnished with emery paper (600 meshes) and washed in acetone by ultrasonic cleaning equipment. The specimens were embedded with epoxy, leaving one of the bases exposed to be used as the test solution. A platinum electrode was used as an auxiliary electrode and a calomel electrode as a reference electrode. The electrolytic cell was maintained at 37•}0.5•Ž . Potentiodynamic polarization was carried out using a potentiostat. After the free corrosion potential was stable, polarization measurement was started from the rest potential at a scan rate of 0.5mV/s and the polarization curve was obtained. The corrosive solutions were 1% NaCl, 1% lactic acid, 0.05% HCl and Greenwood's artificial saliva, deaired by argon purging. 4) Resistance to corrosion of the sealed SmCo5 magnet with stainless steel The magnetic attachment, which was reported in a previous paper22), was used as the Fig. 2 The magnet attachment and its crosssection. 122 A. RESULTS Attractive force change Figure 3 depicts the attractive forces of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets for the different periods of the immersions in artificial saliva and 1% lactic acid. These results were derived form one sample for each kind of magnet. Before the immersion in the artificial saliva, the attractive force between the Nd2Fe14B magnets was 292g. The attractive force decreased to 94% of 292g after one day, and continued to decrease gradually to 88% of 292g at forty-two days of immersion. For the SmCo5 magnets, the attractive force was 227g at the beginning and decreased to 95% of 227g after forty-two days of immersion. Thus the decrease rate of SmCo5 magnets was less than one-half of Nd2Fe14B magnets. The attractive force between Nd2Fe14B magnets was 301g before the immersion in 1% lactic acid. Even after one day of immersion, the attractive force decreased rapidly to become 44% of 301g; it decreased to 28% of 301g after seven days of immersion. The attractive force could not be measured at fourteen days of immersion, because the Nd2Fe14B magnet had lost its shape as the result of corrosion. DISCUSSION In artificial saliva, the attractive force of Nd2Fe14B magnet decreased to only 88% of the initial force even after forty-two days of immersion. In SmCo5 magnets, the attractive force maintained 95% of the initial force. The released amounts of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 126 A. KITSUGI, O. OKUNO, T. NAKANO, H. HAMANAKA and T. KURODA magnets were also very small. Even slight increases of weight that were nevertheless significant (p<0.05) were observed in both the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets in artificial saliva. These decreases of the attractive force were probably due to the formation of corrosive products or adsorption of protein in the saliva on the surface of the magnets; this could be because the attractive force of both magnets recovered 94% and 97% of the initial value, respectively, after their surfaces were thoroughly wiped and cleaned of acetone. The magnets might achieve an even closer proximity by removing corrosion products or adsorbed protein. Taken together, these results indicated that the magnets might not corrode as fast in artificial saliva. The amounts of released elements of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets were less than 10ƒÊg/cm2 in 0.1% Na2S. The reductions of weight of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets were very small in 0.1% Na2S. This suggests that the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets may be not as corrosive in 0.1% Na2S. The amounts of released elements from the SmCo5 magnet in 1% NaCl were slight. On the other hand, those from the Nd2Fe14B magnet were about ten times those of the SmCo5 one. Although the reason for the difference of weight reductions was not clear, the free corrosion potential of the Nd2Fe14B magnet was lower. From these results, the resistance to corrosion of the Nd2Fe14B magnet might be inferior to that of the SmCo5 magnet in 1% NaCl. The amounts of released elements of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets were some hundreds or thousands ƒÊg/cm2 in 0.05% HCl. These amount were at same level as the amount of Ni ions released from the Ni-Cr dental alloy23) in 0.05% HCl. The quantity of weight loss of the SmCo5 magnet was small in 0.05 HCl. In comparison, the Nd2Fe14B magnet decreased greatly, to 0.15g/cm2, and deposits were present in the vials (Fig. 9). This showed that abundant insoluble corrosive products might be produced from the Nd2Fe14B magnet in 0.05% HCl in addition to soluble corrosive products. The Nd2Fe14B magnet was more corrosive than the SmCo5 one in 0.05% HCl. This finding was supported by the results that the free corrosion potential of the Nd2Fe14B magnet was lower than that of the SmCo5 one (a) (b) Fig. 9 0.05% HCl solutions of the magnets immersed for seven days (a) Nd2Fe14B magnet (b) SmCo5 magnet. THE CORROSION BEHAVIOR OF RARE EARTH MAGNETS 127 in 0.05% HCl, as was shown in the anodic polarization measurement. Both the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets were dissolved extensively in 1% lactic acid. The amounts of released elements of the SmCo5 magnet were more than the hundreds of times reported by Nakano et al.18), and our results were also different from those of Tsutsui et al.16) which had indicated that the weight loss in 1% lactic acid was larger than that in 0.05% HCl. This might have been caused by there having been a difference of corrosive resistance between the types of Sm-Co magnets. There are several types of SmCo5 or Sm2Co17 magnets. The amounts of released elements were more than about fifty times those of the Ni ions released from the Ni-Cr alloy in 1% lactic acid23). In the weight change test, there was the great decrease of 0.06-0.10g/cm2 in only one day of immersion. After three days, the rate of weight loss of SmCo5 magnet became slow, but that of the Nd2Fe14B magnet did not change. Even after one day of immersion, the attractive force of the Nd2Fe14B magnet decreased considerably. Both the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets lost their shapes by the actions of the corrosion after fourteen days of immersion. Even in a short period immersion, the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets became strongly corroded in 1% lactic acid. This showed that the rare earth magnets might bear some probability of considerable corrosion in an oral environment. Currently, SmCo5 magnets are being hermetically sealed within stainless steel capsules by means of laser welding. The disadvantage of corrosion in rare earth magnets can be overcome by putting them into such stainless steel capsules followed by laser welding. The magnetic attachments in this study were examined under immersions in 1% NaCl, and their being sealed with laser-welded stainless steel capsule was effective although this immersion was a relatively mild environment. It is hoped that these samples will be examined under more severe conditions. The tested magnetic attachment was developed for being used in prosthetics. It will be also necessary for rare earth magnets to be hermetically sealed within stainless steel capsules for orthodontic use, even though it will be required during a shorter period compared to use in prosthetics. CONCLUSION The corrosion behavior of rare earth magnets in an oral environment was investigated by means of the attractive force change, release of elements, weight change and anodic polarization measurements in 1% NaCl, 1% lactic acid, 0.05% HCl, 0.1% Na2S and Greenwood's artificial saliva at 37•Ž. In artificial saliva, the attractive force of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets was decreased to about 90% of the initial attractive force after forty-two days of immersions. The released amounts were very small and their weights increased slightly. It was considered that the corrosion of both the magnets might not progress faster in ordinary oral conditions. The corrosive changes in 1% NaCl and 0.1% Na2S were also not noteworthy. In 1% lactic acid, the attractive force of the Nd2Fe14B and SmCo5 magnets decreased within a short period of time during the immersions, and the released amounts were large. Their weights were reduced greatly by the immersions in 1% lactic acid. Both the Nd2Fe14B magnet and the SmCo5 magnet were very corrosive in 1% lactic acid, and also suffered 128 A. The corrosive activity of the Nd2Fe14B magnet was higher than that of the SmCo5 magnet in every corrosive solution. It was necessary that the rare earth magnets were hermetically sealed with laser-welded stainless steel capsules for use in the fields of dentistry. After implantation or soaking, the specimens were characterized by scanning electron microscopic analyses, X-ray diffractometry, and infrared absorption spectroscopy. X-ray diffraction study showed that OCP had been completely transformed to apatite with low crystallinity such as the mouse's femur after a 3 -week implantation in the mouse body , and an apatic crystal was formed after soaking in the NaCl solution. The IR absorption spectra revealed that CO3 was incorporated in the apatite formed from OCP in both the mouse body and the NaCl solution, while OCP changed little after soaking in the SBF. It seems that the magnesium ion retards the transformation of OCP to apatite. Key words: Octacalcium phosphate, Hydroxyapatite, Phase transformation INTRODUCTION Calcium phosphate ceramics sometimes display bone growth guiding properties, causing bone to grow into areas that it would otherwise not occupy, although they do not induce bone formation in the traditional sense. Octacalcium phosphate (Ca8 H2 (PO4)6•E5H2O, hereafter referred to as OCP) occurs in pathological calcifications, frequently as one of the crystalline components of human dental calculi1,2). OCP has been also presumed a necessary precursor of biological apatites in both normal (enamel, dentine, cementum, and bones) and pathological (e.g., phosphatic renal stones) calcifications3,4,5). It is known that OCP transforms to hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2, hereafter referred to as HA) in a neutral pH region6,7,8). On the other hand, we developed a new preparation method for a quick preparation of a large amount of OCP by reactions of dicalcium phosphate dihydrate (CaHPO4•E2H2O, hereafter referred to as DCPD) and calcium carbonate (CaCO3)9). It was found that OCP was formed on the crystal plate of DCPD, and was converted to HA with time. The present study was undertaken in an attempt to investigate in vivo and in vitro phase transformation of the OCP synthesized by our preparation method. It has been suggested that magnesium has a great influence on the rate of transformation and precipitation of calcium phosphate6,10,11). Therefore, physiological solutions with and without magnesium were used in soaking media in vitro. The products transformed from OCP were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffractometry, infrared spectroscopy and energy dispersive X-ray micro-analysis. PHASE TRANSFORMATION OF OCTACALCIUM PHOSPHATE 131 MATERIALS AND METHODS OCP was synthesized by the chemical reaction of a suspension of DCPD and CaCO3. HASEGAWA DISCUSSION The characterization analysis carried out in this study demonstrated that OCP was completely transformed to carbonate apatite with low crystallinity in the mouse body and that it contained small amounts of Na and Mg. From the EDX spectra in Fig. 5, the ratios of Ca, Na and Mg to P of the product were calculated to 1.18•}0.07, 0.018•}0.002, and 0.036•} 0.004, respectively, whereas these ratios in the femur were 1.52•}0.08, 0.012•}0.003, and 0. 028•}0.004, respectively. The Ca/P ratio of the OCP after implantation is smaller than that of the femur and calcium phosphates deposited on the bioactive ceramics in vivo19,20) and in vitro12,13,21). It seems that the substitutions of Ca by Mg, Na in OCP are large, subsequently causing the Ca/P ratio to decrease in value. OCP changed little in the SBF, whereas OCP was completely transformed to apatite in 1% NaCl solution. It seems that the Mg in the SBF retarded the transformation of OCP to apatite. It is well known that Mg2+ ion competes with Ca2+ ion (or CaOH+) for being exchanged with the H+ ion of the precipitate10), and the incorporation of Mg2+ ions into calcium phosphate can retard the transformation of amorphous calcium phosphate, such as calcium deficient hydroxyapatite11,22). One hypothesis has been that Mg occurs in a whitlockite phase, Ca9Mg(HPO4)(PO4)6, with ultimate composition23,24). On the other hand, CO32- ions replace PO43- ions in their structure18,21), and incorporation of CO32- ions also retards the crystallization of amorphous calcium phosphate20). These substitutions might well be coupled to each other to maintain electrical neutrality17). The substitutions of ions in the product are strongly related to the composition of the surrounding solution. This supports the proposition that the mineral phase of bone is controlled by the physiochemical equilibrium between bone and blood plasma. In this physiochemical equilibrium, at least the ions of Ca2+, PO43-, Na+, Mg2+, carbonate and citrate, and perhaps those of Cl-, SO42-, Sr2+, and F- as well, are involved. Although OCP contained Mg2+ and CO32- after implantation in the mouse, OCP was completely transformed to carbonate apatite after a 3-week implantation. This suggests that the transformation of OCP in vivo is accelerated by other factors. For instance, it is known that fluoride in vitro accelerates the hydrolysis of OCP to apatite5,25). Furthermore, calcium phosphate ceramics in movable soft tissue induce inflammation by a kind of foreign body reaction with the characteristic signs of fibrous encapsulation and giant cell reaction26). Therefore, it is concluded that the transformation of OCP in vivo is due to not only inorganic chemical reactions with body fluid but also results from physiological reactions. The dental material used in the mouth must resist not only a single large force but also repeated small forces during mastication. The repeated stress sometimes results in fatigue fractures. Preparation of the test piece for this method was not difficult, and it was also possible to embed a screw directly into the test material. This new tensile fatigue test is a precrack fatigue test because the terminal edge of the screw acts as a precrack. As a result, the crack propagation of each tested specimen was initiated from the terminal edge of the screw. On the other hand, with the photoelastic test, some researchers11-13) reported that an applied stress caused stress concentration around the terminal edge of the screw post. Our observation of the initial crack position agreed with a previously reported position of stress concentration. The mechanical properties, such as compressive strength and diametral strength, of the zinc oxide eugenol cement were weaker than those of the zinc phosphate cement18). CONCLUSION A new tensile fatigue test method with a stainless steel screw was introduced. By this method, actual fatigue fractures occurred in the acrylic test specimen. The number of times the cyclic load was applied the crack was initiated and when the final fracture occurred varied with the applied waveform. The more favorable waveform of applied load was considered to be the cyclic haver-triangles load. Luting of the screw with a cement strengthened the fatigue properties; therefore, it was considered better for the screw to be cemented or be directly embedded into the tested material. The type of cement had an effect on the fatigue properties; however, the difference of numbers of times of applied load between the initiate crack and the final fracture with cementation using zinc oxide eugenol cement and that using the zinc phosphate cement was nearly the same. It was constructed with a thermocycle loading line and a leakage detecting line partitioned from each other by the restoration under evaluation. The hot and cold solutions of rhodamine B as a tracer were alternately circulated in the thermocycle loading line by the switching of six solenoid valves. Marginal leakage of the tracer into distilled water circulating in the detecting line was periodically monitored by a spectrometer while thermocyling the restoration. Key words: Marginal seal, Thermal cycling, Serial monitoring INTRODUCTION It has been accepted for decades that marginal sealing is a very important property in dental restorations. Such marginal seals are ordinary evaluated by measuring the extent of marginal leakage. As reviewed in the literatures by Iwaku1) and Zardiackas2), this leakage has been estimated by a wide variety of techniques including the use of dyes, radioisotope or bacterial penetration, electrical methods, scanning electron microscopy and clinical observations. A serial in vitro technique providing more quantitative data would be beneficial to screen the marginal sealing capability of restorative materials. As long as there is no information on the relation between the damage caused by leakage and the width and extent of a marginal gap, no gap of any size would be acceptable. Therefore, the most important factor in serial measurement of marginal leakage is how long the restoration maintains a complete seal. We devised a new method for estimating the duration of complete marginal sealing against thermocycling. In this paper, the developed testing system, procedures and some applications will be reported. MATERIALS AND METHODS Fundamental preparation of the tooth specimen (Fig, 1-a) A flat square plate (ca. 10•~10•~2mm) was obtained from a bovine anterior tooth by sectioning and grinding under a stream of water. The tooth plate consisting of enamel and A NEW METHOD FOR MARGINAL SEAL ASSESSMENT 151 dentin was mounted in a photo-cured unfilled resin to make a disc 20mm in diameter. Both surfaces of the resinous disc were slightly polished to confirm exposure of the tooth. A perforation of 3mm in diameter was prepared in the tooth plate for use as a restoring cavity in the usual way. After the hole was restored with a material, the specimen surfaces were polished again to remove any excess of the material. Clamping the specimen (Fig. 1-b) First, the specimen was sandwiched between two silicone rubber sheets each having a hole 4mm in diameter. The specimen was covered with the silicone rubbers, leaving 0.5mm around the enamel and dentin margins of the restoration. The sandwich (ca. 3.5mm thick) was put in a 3-mm deep basin of a stainless steel specimen holder. When the holder was closed by four locking bolts, the tooth specimen was tightly brought in full contact to the holder while being mediated by silicone rubbers. The enamel side surface of the clamped specimen was oriented to the thermocycling line described below. System design A schematic drawing of the developed testing system is shown in Fig. 2. A NEW METHOD FOR MARGINAL SEAL ASSESSMENT 155 DISCUSSION Most of the techniques of leakage measurement require that tooth be destroyed at the time of evaluation. The electrical method5,6) is one representative quantified technique allowing serial monitoring. However, this method is limited to electrically nonconductive restorative material. Derkson et al.7) reported another long-term monitoring technique; they detected the passage of a fluid from the pulp to the cavosurface under a certain pressure. Leakage into the marginal area from the cavosurface is not directly evaluated using Derkson's technique. Powis et al.8) dealt with serial leakage data based on Fick's diffusion law to estimate the interfacial gap area. Only the gaps that had existed prior to the measurement or had been formed due to dissolution of the material could be detected in their method since the samples are maintained isothermally in an aqueous medium at all times. Our leakage measuring technique serves as in vitro screening of marginal sealing capability of dental restorations. There are some advantages: serial monitoring of dynamic leakage is possible on a restoration being thermocycled, metallic, organic and inorganic restorative materials can be tested, and the collected quantitative data can be analyzed to estimate how long a complete seal can be maintained against thermocycling. We consider that until the acceptable size of the marginal gap is clarified, the durability of complete marginal sealing is the most important factor for dental restorations. Our technique, of course, can be improved upon or be modified in some testing conditions including the use of tracers, leakage-detecting methods and thermocycle conditions. The following considerations were made to assume Eq. 1. First, Nb should be estimated as a thermocycle near No. Second, it is expected that CN finally reaches a maximum, Cmax, when leakages are regarded as the gradual mixing of a concentrated solution to a diluted one. Lastly, the data can be processed by simple linear analysis. Nevertheless, it should be noted that Eq. 1 is a tentative formula. Although Eq. 1 has well explained the leakage data shown here, it would be desirable, if possible, to devise a theoretical formula on leakage behavior under thermal cycling. However, marginal sealability may be affected by complicated factors. Physical parameters of restorative materials are not the sole factors influencing marginal leakage behavior9). Further measurements are required to establish a more solid, empirical formula. CONCLUSIONS A new methodology for the assessment of marginal sealability was made available by the development of a testing system. Marginal leakage during thermal cycling could be monitored and analyzed to estimate the durability of complete marginal sealing against thermal change. DISCUSSION Since shape memory effect and super-elasticity of Ni-Ti alloy are the phenomena caused by martensitic transformation and the associated reverse transformation, transformation temperatures of the Ni-Ti alloy have a great influence on its mechanical properties. The shape memory effect is observed when a deformed shape recovers by heating above the Af point, and super-elasticity is observed when a deformation above the Af point over the elatic limit recovers by being unloaded. In this study, the influence of the composition and the purity of titanium on the tensile properties and the transformation temperatures of Ni-Ti alloy castings were investigated with the aim of applying the alloy castings in dental prostheses or appliances . The tested composition range was 49.0-49.2at% titanium in forming the alloy ingots with the expectation of super-elasticity. The selected grades of titanium were those of highest purity , because the properties of Ni-Ti alloy are known to be very sensitive to impurities21) . The influence of the titanium's purity on the tensile properties of Ni-Ti alloy castings is similar to that of the composition as shown in Figs. 1-4. The tensile properties of Ni-49.2Ti alloy castings with the titanium of lower purity resembled those of a lower titanium content of 49.0-49.1at%. It is thought that this change in tensile properties is mainly caused by the change in transformation temperatures. Lower titanium content and deterioration of titanium purity lowered the MS and Af points, as shown in Table 2. The deterioration of titanium purity from SSU to S-90 is presumed to be about 0.1mass%, taken from the data in Table 1. Accordingly, the decrease of titanium content in the composition of Ni-49.2Ti alloy is estimated to be around 0.05at%. This agrees with the reduction of transformation temperatures shown in Table 2. It is known that the reduction of transformation temperatures also occurs by the presence of impurities, e.g., oxygen, carbon and 3d transition metals21) . The apparent proof strength of the Ni-Ti alloy increased with decreasing titanium content. The main reason for this change is thought to be the lowered martensitic transformation temperature range, according to the Clausius-Clapeyron relation22) . No significant change as the result of titanium content was recognized in the tensile strength of the Ni-Ti alloy; however, a clear difference was observed in the mode of its appearance , as depicted in Figs. 1 and 3. The tensile strength of specimens with the lower titanium content appeared at relatively small elongation after the apparent proof strength , while that of specimens with the higher titanium content appeared at a large elongation after the plateau of stress-induced martensitic transformation. The Af points of the tested Ni -Ti alloy castings were lower than 310K , the tensile testing temperature. However, the shape recovery temperature in the tensile test seems somewhat higher than the Af point obtained by DSC, since an excessive driving force is possibly needed for achieving reverse transformation in testing under severe conditions. CONCLUSION Low titanium content in Ni-Ti alloy casting caused high apparent proof strength, low residual strain and low elongation because of the reduction of transformation temperatures. Small reductions in titanium purity influenced the tensile properties and the transformation temperatures as well. Precise composition and high purity of materials are necessary to control the special and sensitive properties of Ni-Ti alloy castings.
